CHAPTER 1: THE PATTERN OF RETURN (Section B: Christianity - Origins and Contemporary Expressions)

BIG IDEA
- People and groups often look back to their origins (where they came from) to understand the present and find direction for the future.
- Christianity has a regular "pattern of returning" to its origins - going back to the founding vision of Jesus - especially at times of change and turmoil.
- These returns bring new life to the Church, but they also cause upheaval and change.

KEY TERMS (in bold in the chapter)
- Pattern of returning: the repeated way Christianity goes back to its origins (the vision of Jesus) to rediscover and renew itself.
- Founding vision: the original purpose or inspiration of a group. For Christians it is the life, death and resurrection of Jesus as recorded in the Bible, especially the New Testament.
- Mission statement: a summary of an organisation's core values, aims and objectives.
- Mendicant orders: "begging orders" - religious orders from the 13th century whose members owned nothing and had the right to beg.
- Heresy: a belief or teaching that goes against the official teaching of the Church.
- Excommunicated: officially cut off from the Church.
- Evangelical: a trend in Christianity that pays particular attention to the place of scripture in the life of a Christian.
- Transdenominational: found across many different denominations (the word "evangelical" is transdenominational).
- Denominations: different Christian churches or groups (e.g. Catholic, Anglican, Methodist).
- Ethics: the study of right and wrong; how we should behave.
- Methodism: an evangelical movement and church founded by John Wesley with his brother Charles.
- Aggiornamento: Italian word meaning "updating" - the purpose of Vatican II, to update the Church.
- Liberation theology: a way of interpreting and living the gospel in the light of the experience of the poor, working to free people from poverty and oppression.
- Preferential option for the poor: the decision that the Church would be on the side of the poor and work to transform society.

PART 1: THE RETURN TO ORIGINS
- Opening quote: Irish youth at World Youth Day Festival, Cologne 2005: "They say religion is difficult in times of prosperity... 'You can't buy happiness.'"
- By studying the past we learn about ourselves as individuals, family members, members of a nation or religious group.
- This helps us evaluate the present and imagine the future.
- It is part of the human condition to want to learn about the past.

EXAMPLE: THE EMIGRANT'S SEARCH FOR ROOTS
- Every year people of Irish ancestry return to Ireland from all over the world to explore their origins.
- They ask: Where did our ancestors come from? How did they live? Why did they leave?
- Answers help them understand themselves.
- Example: knowing your ancestors survived the Irish famine may affect your attitude to the suffering of others.
- Ireland's reputation for great generosity to famine victims worldwide is linked to its own famine in the nineteenth century.
- Customs, rules and practices often make no sense without knowing their origins.

STORY: THE TRIBE AND THE LIONS
- A thousand years ago a mountain tribe was attacked at night by lions, which killed the weak and elderly in huts at the edge of the village.
- They built a fence around the village with one gate. Nobody was responsible for closing the gate, so it was left open and people were still killed.
- They decided the second son of each family would take turns closing the gate. No more people were killed.
- About a hundred years later the hunters had killed all the lions. Two hundred years after that nobody remembered there had been lions.
- Second sons still close the gate and ask why. Fathers answer: "Because we always have, that's just the way things are."
- Lesson: a tradition can lose its meaning when people forget its origin. Returning to origins explains why we do things.

STORYTELLING
- We look back all the time: photographs, reunions, stories at Christmas, birthdays and funerals.
- Storytelling is the most common way we explore our origins.
- Stories link us to the past, explain how we got here, make sense of the present, and may offer direction for the future, especially when we feel lost.

STORY: THE COLLEGE BAND (SARAH AND "ORIGIN")
- Sarah loved music and playing guitar; writing songs was her real passion. She wanted a career in music.
- She joined a college band called Origin (Luke and three others) after an audition and a try-out period.
- Their first gig was a free one in college during rag week; performing her own song was Sarah's high point.
- Luke announced a paid weekly Thursday night slot in a club - but the manager wanted covers (classics and chart songs), not original songs.
- Sarah realised this was not right for her - her founding reason for joining (writing and playing her own songs) would be lost. She decided she would have to leave.
- Lesson: when a group drifts from the reason you joined, you must return to your original vision, even if it costs you.

THE PURPOSE OF RETURNING: REDISCOVERING THE FOUNDING VISION
- Humans form groups for many reasons - economic, social, religious.
- When we feel unhappy or dissatisfied in a group we need to think about its purpose. We ask:
- Why did we join? Why stay? What does belonging mean to me? Have I changed since joining?
- This helps us rediscover the energy and commitment that first led us to the group.
- It takes great courage, because there is much to lose in security and familiarity.
- People often ask these fundamental questions in times of crisis.

MISSION STATEMENTS
- Most companies, businesses and institutions have a mission statement: a summary of core values, aims and objectives.
- It is formed through consultation with many sources (e.g. a school's should have input from the whole school community).
- Sample mission statement in the chapter: "Our mission is to strengthen the well-being of children and their families, thereby contributing to safe and healthy communities..."
- To be effective, the group must constantly revisit and evaluate it in the light of experience - they must "return to origins".
- Examples: a hospital checks it is providing basic healthcare to the area; a business checks all employees are treated equally.
- The mission statement guides progress and change; it may itself need to be changed.
- Returning to it can cause upheaval and change, but can also bring development and more energy and commitment.

THE CHRISTIAN CHURCH RETURNING TO ORIGINS
- The Church's founding vision is the life, death and resurrection of Jesus as recorded in the Bible, especially the New Testament.
- The Church is a historical institution affected by many movements; each generation brings something new.
- It has suffered division and scandal, and has built up a rich tradition to guide it.
- Many movements in the Church seek to return to the founding vision.

BIBLE-STUDY GROUPS
- Local groups work towards a deeper understanding of the scriptures; many want to "get back to basics" and follow Jesus' teachings.
- Through study and prayer they reflect on how the scriptures speak to them today.
- This may lead to seeing things in a new way or challenging their church from within.

SMALL CHRISTIAN COMMUNITIES
- Christians worldwide live in small Christian communities to live as the early Christians lived and reconnect with the foundational experience.
- For some, being a member of a parish felt like alienation; others wanted to live the Christian message more radically.
- Essential qualities:
- A living cell, an integral part of the Church; the core group that galvanises (energises) wider communities.
- Sharing all aspects of life: spiritual (prayer, Word of God, Eucharist), intellectual (ideas), emotional (friendship), material (earthly goods), apostolic (work).
- Fits the vision of Church as People of God - emphasis on people, not organisation or buildings.
- Justice - right relationships with God, neighbour and the environment - is a major concern.
- Priority to promoting the Kingdom of God - harmony rooted deeply in justice.
- James O'Halloran, "Happiness is Belonging": the staple parts of a meeting are worship (Scripture, prayer, Eucharist), community (fellowship) and reality (keeping in touch with life); meetings should be functional and flexible.
- Link to the early Church, Acts 4:32,34: "Now the whole group of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common... There was not a needy person among them."
- Effect: they breathe new life into the wider community and may challenge the way things are.

REDISCOVERY AND REFORM AS A PATTERN OF CHRISTIANITY
- Christianity is founded on the vision of Jesus Christ and regularly returns to origins to rediscover it.
- The chapter looks at movements from the eighth to the twentieth century.
- Many happened at times of change and turmoil in society - people tend to question a group's purpose when life is difficult.
- Effect: new life for the Church, but also upheaval and change.

THE CEILI DE (THE CULDEES) - 8TH CENTURY, IRELAND
- The eighth century was a time of great change; 800 years had passed since Jesus' death.
- Emerged around the second half of the eighth century in Ireland; at the same time as European reform movements but uniquely Irish.
- Begun by Maelruain and Dudlittir, abbots of monasteries in Tallaght and Finglas.
- Came from dissatisfaction with monastic life among some religious, and disenchantment with how Christians generally lived.
- Main focus: renewal of the monastic tradition, which reformers believed had lost its way.
- Special emphasis on study and the hermetic (hermit) life; produced a large body of literature.
- Reform through re-emphasising Prayer, Labour and Study - "the three profitable things in the day".
- Monks prayed for at least eight hours a day: Night Vigil, Morning/Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, Compline.
- Many prayers said with arms outstretched.
- Rest of the day: studying and writing devotional literature, often religious poetry.
- Vows of poverty and perpetual chastity.
- Concerned about the falling off of religious practice among the people; stressed Sunday as a day of rest and prayer (not strictly kept at the time).
- Never highly structured, did not develop uniformly, so it has not survived.

THE MENDICANT ORDERS - 13TH CENTURY
- Mendicant = begging orders; a reform movement within the Church in the thirteenth century.
- Grew out of disillusionment with the Church.
- Growth of towns/urban centres in the 12th and 13th centuries led to exchange of ideas and a climate of questioning.
- Christians saw the clergy as a select, very powerful and wealthy group whose lifestyle did not match gospel values.
- Many movements criticised Church abuses; many were accused of heresy and excommunicated.
- The Mendicant orders stayed firmly within the Church, embraced poverty, and worked to uproot false teachings among a disenchanted laity.
- The Church saw them as a fortunate development.
- They developed an urban form of monastic life close to the lifestyle of Jesus in the Gospels.
- Three common characteristics:
- As individuals they held no possessions and had the right to beg.
- All members of an order were united, regardless of location.
- Pastoral care was the focus of their training.
- Four Mendicant orders: Dominicans, Franciscans, Augustinians, Carmelites.

THE DOMINICANS
- Founded by St Dominic, from Castile in Spain, born 1170.
- Travelled through Languedoc in France in 1203; concerned at the amount of heresy there.
- Believed in preaching and pious example; founded a group committed to absolute poverty and preaching the gospel.
- Recognised in 1216 by Pope Honorius III; known as the Order of Preachers.
- Emphasised learning; influential in medieval universities of Europe.

THE FRANCISCANS
- Founded by St Francis of Assisi (1181-1226), son of a wealthy merchant.
- At twenty he renounced his wealth for a life of poverty and preaching.
- Did not intend to found an order, but young men inspired by his commitment to the poor followed him to imitate Christ in all things.
- Officially recognised by Pope Honorius III in 1223.
- Particularly effective in preaching to the poor; also influential in universities.

MARTIN LUTHER - 16TH CENTURY, THE REFORMATION
- The 15th and 16th centuries: great change and creativity (politics, science, art, literature, philosophy) - the Renaissance.
- The Church also experienced change and reform - the Reformation.
- Luther was a German Augustinian priest, aware of the gap between the early Church and the lifestyle of church leaders.
- 1510: travelled to Rome for his priory; appalled by the immorality, laziness and lack of religious commitment among popes and hierarchy.
- Struggled with a great sense of his own unworthiness.
- 1515: breakthrough while reading St Paul's letter to the Romans: "The one who is righteous will live by faith." (Romans 1:17)
- He believed God's love is a gift available to us if we have faith; it cannot be earned; we cannot save ourselves. God's forgiveness is a gift to those who have faith in God through Jesus Christ.
- He said this was not his own idea but was found in St Paul and St Augustine.
- Implications for the medieval Church: if salvation is by faith alone, what role for the clergy as mediators? For the sacraments? Why obtain indulgences?
- 1517: nailed ninety-five theses (arguments) against indulgences and pilgrimages to the door of the Castle Church at Wittenberg.
- His aim was theological debate, not rebellion. He never got to debate with the hierarchy but gained much support in Germany.
- June 1520: Pope Leo X condemned his views, ordered his books burned, gave him two months to retract or be guilty of heresy.
- 1521 Diet of Worms: Luther refused to retract and was excommunicated; named a heretic in 1521.
- The Diet would have accepted him if he had retracted his doctrines on faith and worked from within.
- He fled to Wartburg castle in Saxony under the protection of Frederick the Wise.
- This began the split between the Roman Catholic Church and Luther's supporters - the Reformation. Many other reformers followed.

JOHN WESLEY AND METHODISM - 18TH/19TH CENTURY
- Evangelical: a trend paying particular attention to scripture in Christian life; transdenominational.
- Key characteristics of evangelical movements:
- Scripture is the ultimate guide for spirituality and ethics.
- Particular emphasis on the saving death of Jesus Christ on the cross.
- Personal conversion leading to a change in how one lives.
- Concern for sharing the Christian faith is paramount.
- Methodism developed in the late 18th and early 19th century; founded by John Wesley (1703-91) with his brother Charles.
- They never meant to found a new church, but to develop societies where people could improve their spiritual nature.
- Wesley stressed a "living faith" and the role of experience in Christian life.
- Began with a group of Oxford students wanting a disciplined method of spiritual improvement: regular private devotions, daily scripture reading and prayer.
- Grew from a small group of friends into an important revivalist movement.
- Wesley never meant to leave the Church of England, but Methodism grew to look different from the Anglican Church; part of a religious revival in 19th-century England.
- In time it broke away from the Church of England and became a distinct denomination.
- Most characteristic feature: the need for personal holiness.
- Strong emphasis on joining personal faith with social action (the gospel is both personal and social).
- Strong role for the laity, seen clearly in its structure of government.
- Result: a revival within Protestantism in the nineteenth century.

THE SECOND VATICAN COUNCIL (VATICAN II), 1962-65
- Two major 20th-century events influenced radical reform in the Catholic Church: Vatican II (1962-65) and the Council of Latin American Bishops at Medellin (1968).
- The first Vatican Council was 1869-70.
- Unlike the other reforms, Vatican II came from the centre of power and authority in the Church. Other movements came from the margins and were often seen as a threat.
- Called by Pope John XXIII in 1962.
- Context: the 1960s - a time of hope and change; civil rights movement worldwide (Black people in North America, women everywhere, Catholics in Northern Ireland); student protests; the peace movement.
- Pope John XXIII saw the need to read the signs of the times and discern the Church's role in the 20th century.
- Purpose: aggiornamento (updating) - "throwing open the windows and letting the winds of change blow through the Church".
- Began October 1962; four sessions over four years; more than 2,450 bishops from all over the world; also non-Catholic observers, Catholic men and women auditors, and journalists.
- Pope John XXIII died on 3 June 1963; the Council was continued by Pope Paul VI.
- Produced sixteen documents.
- Dogmatic Constitution on the Church (Lumen gentium): the Church should see itself more as a community of believers than a hierarchical institution.
- Called for more active involvement of the laity.
- Considered relations with other religions; stressed reconciling with other churches.
- Stressed the social side of faith: human rights, race relations and social justice.
- Changes: Mass said in the local language instead of Latin; priest facing the people; rules on religious dress relaxed; laity more involved in the sacraments.
- Caused excitement and hope but also fear; some felt tradition was threatened, so tension arose. Many say the tension was healthy and creative.
- Greatest legacy: it paved the way for discussion and discernment and gave hope to those who felt isolated.

LIBERATION THEOLOGY - 1968 ONWARDS
- Vatican II's Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World (Gaudium et spes) called the Church to examine the signs of the times and interpret them in the light of the gospel - to work against injustice.
- Liberation theology grew out of this challenge.
- Launched in 1968 at a congress of Latin American bishops at Medellin in Colombia, to take up Vatican II's challenge.
- A radical new way of interpreting and living the gospel in the light of the experience of the poor of Latin America.
- The bishops concluded Latin American society was unjust - most people lived in poverty and oppression.
- The Church would be on the side of the poor and work to transform society so all could live in dignity and freedom: the preferential option for the poor.
- 1971: Gustavo Gutierrez, a Peruvian theologian, wrote "A Theology of Liberation", outlining the theory and its roots in the gospel.
- Supporters believe the story of God's people is a story of liberation from oppression, the gospel is a message of liberation, and Jesus is the great liberator. Working for justice is truly following Jesus.
- It upset people in power; many rich Latin Americans were devout Catholics but did not want the political or economic status quo disturbed.
- Some activists were tortured or killed; most famous was Archbishop Oscar Romero, murdered in March 1980.
- Critics: too concerned with this world and not the next; too political and not spiritual enough.
- Supporters: it is firmly rooted in the example of Jesus Christ. A powerful example of reform from within the Church.

FOR REFLECTION
- Philippians 1:27-30: St Paul's advice to the early Christians at Philippi to live in a way "worthy of the Gospel of Christ".
- The movements studied span twelve centuries, all trying to be worthy of the Gospel.

SUMMARY TIMELINE
- 8th century: Ceili De (Ireland) - Maelruain and Dudlittir.
- 13th century: Mendicant orders - Dominicans (recognised 1216), Franciscans (1223).
- 1517: Luther's 95 theses; 1521 Diet of Worms and excommunication.
- Late 18th/19th century: John Wesley and Methodism.
- 1962-65: Vatican II.
- 1968: Medellin; 1971: Gutierrez's book; 1980: Romero murdered.

COMMON THREADS (useful for exam answers)
- Each movement grew from dissatisfaction or a sense that the Church had lost its way.
- Each looked back to the founding vision of Jesus or the early Church (poverty, scripture, community, justice).
- Most arose at times of social change and turmoil (cultural context shapes Christianity).
- Each brought new life but also upheaval and change.
- Most came from the margins; Vatican II came from the centre.

rows.prompt: Outline two reasons why a group or organisation might need to return to its founding vision. Refer to an example in your answer.
rows.model_answer:
Groups need to return to their founding vision when members feel unhappy or dissatisfied. By asking 'Why did we join? Why stay? What does belonging mean to me?', members can rediscover the energy and commitment that first led them to join. For example, Sarah joined the band Origin because writing songs was her passion. When the club manager wanted only covers, she returned to her original reason for joining and realised she had to leave.

A second reason is to check progress and make changes. Many organisations have a mission statement summarising their core values and aims. For it to be effective, the group must constantly revisit it in the light of experience. A hospital might check if it is really providing basic healthcare to its area, or a business might check if all employees are treated equally. This process can cause upheaval and change, but it can also lead to development and new energy and commitment. Such questions are often asked in times of crisis, and it takes courage because there is much to lose in security and familiarity.

rows.prompt: Discuss how the Mendicant orders were an example of a return to origins within Christianity.
rows.model_answer:
In the thirteenth century the growth of towns led to an exchange of ideas and a climate of questioning. Christians looked critically at their clergy and saw a powerful, wealthy group whose lifestyle bore little resemblance to the gospel. Many protest movements were accused of heresy and excommunicated, but the Mendicant or begging orders stayed firmly within the Church.

They returned to origins by developing an urban form of religious life close to the lifestyle of Jesus in the Gospels. As individuals they held no possessions and had the right to beg; all members were united regardless of location; and pastoral care was the focus of their training. They embraced poverty and worked to uproot false teachings among the disenchanted laity.

St Dominic, born in Castile in 1170, was concerned by heresy in Languedoc in 1203 and founded an order committed to absolute poverty and preaching, recognised by Pope Honorius III in 1216 as the Order of Preachers. St Francis of Assisi, son of a wealthy merchant, renounced his wealth at twenty to imitate Christ in all things; his followers were recognised in 1223 and were especially effective in preaching to the poor. Both orders brought new life to the Church by living the gospel simply, as Jesus had.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: urban growth and questioning; wealth of clergy contradicting gospel; other movements accused of heresy; Mendicants stayed within Church; three characteristics (no possessions/right to beg, unity, pastoral care); four orders; Dominic (Castile 1170, Languedoc 1203, Order of Preachers 1216); Francis (1181-1226, renounced wealth, 1223, preaching to poor); link to lifestyle of Jesus.

rows.prompt: Describe the role of Martin Luther as a reformer who sought to return the Church to its origins.
rows.model_answer:
Martin Luther was a German Augustinian priest who lived during the Renaissance, a time of questioning and change. He was conscious of the great gap between the early Church and the lifestyle of church leaders. In 1510 he travelled to Rome and was appalled by the immorality, laziness and lack of religious commitment of the popes and hierarchy.

Luther struggled with his own unworthiness until 1515, when he read in Romans 1:17 that 'The one who is righteous will live by faith.' He came to believe that God's love and forgiveness are a free gift to those who have faith in Jesus Christ and cannot be earned. He said this idea came from St Paul and St Augustine - a return to the Church's origins. This raised questions about the role of clergy, sacraments and indulgences.

In 1517 he nailed ninety-five theses against indulgences and pilgrimages to the door of the Castle Church at Wittenberg, hoping for debate, not rebellion. He gained support in Germany, but in 1520 Pope Leo X condemned his views and ordered his books burned. At the Diet of Worms in 1521 he refused to retract and was excommunicated. He fled to Wartburg castle under Frederick the Wise. This began the split that gave rise to the Reformation.

rows.prompt: 'Vatican II and liberation theology were both responses to the signs of the times.' Discuss this statement.
rows.model_answer:
Vatican II (1962-65) was called by Pope John XXIII in the 1960s, a time of hope and change when the civil rights movement, student protests and the peace movement were growing. The Pope saw the need to read the signs of the times and update the Church - aggiornamento - by throwing open the windows to let the winds of change blow through. Over 2,450 bishops met in four sessions and produced sixteen documents. Lumen gentium presented the Church as a community of believers; the laity were given a bigger role; Mass was said in the local language with the priest facing the people; and the Council stressed human rights, social justice and dialogue with other churches. Unusually, this reform came from the centre of the Church.

Vatican II's Gaudium et spes called on Christians to examine the signs of the times in the light of the gospel. Liberation theology grew from this. In 1968 Latin American bishops at Medellin concluded that their society was unjust, as most people lived in poverty and oppression. They declared a preferential option for the poor. In 1971 Gustavo Gutierrez wrote A Theology of Liberation, presenting Jesus as the great liberator. It upset the powerful, and Archbishop Oscar Romero was murdered in 1980. Both show the Church responding to its context by returning to the gospel.
